text: Why can a class implement many interfaces but extend only one class?
choices: Because interfaces are erased at compile time, so only the class survives to run time.
Because the JVM's method tables have a fixed number of slots for superclasses.
Interfaces carry no state, so combining several creates nothing to conflict; combining implementations would.
Because multiple inheritance was considered too confusing for the language's audience.
explanation: Multiple inheritance of implementation raises the question of what happens when two parents define the same field or supply the same method body. Multiple inheritance of *contract* has no such problem: two interfaces both demanding `draw()` is one demand made twice. The restriction is about state — which is also why `default` methods, which added bodies, came with careful rules for resolving conflicts.
